text: You already know what a correlation coefficient is from the statistics course. This lesson is about using it as an EDA tool: scanning a whole table for relationships, picking the right kind of correlation, and knowing when the number is lying to you.

dataframe dot corr computes every pairwise correlation at once. Plot it as a heatmap with a diverging scale fixed from negative one to one, so colors mean the same thing every time. Tenure and orders are the strongest pair at zero point five five. Tenure and churned sit at negative zero point one eight, a weak negative link. Age sits near zero against everything.

Pearson measures linear association and is sensitive to extreme values. Spearman correlates the ranks instead, so it captures any rising or falling relationship and shrugs off outliers. Look at orders versus total spend: Pearson says only zero point two oh, but Spearman says zero point eight five. That's a huge gap for the same two columns.

The cause is the two extreme spend values, seventy-four hundred and ninety-eight hundred. Drop just those two rows out of five hundred, and Pearson jumps to zero point eight one. Two rows dragged the coefficient from point eight one down to point two oh.

The lesson: whenever Pearson and Spearman disagree sharply, look for outliers or a curved relationship, and plot the pair before trusting either number. A correlation with a zero-one column like churned works for a quick scan, but grouped comparisons are usually more readable for a yes-no outcome.

Correlation can't tell you about causation; tenure correlates with orders, but which direction, or is something else behind both? It misses non-linear patterns, a U-shape can score near zero. And a small correlation might still matter for a large population while a large one might not matter for one decision.
Use corr and an annotated diverging heatmap to scan many pairs quickly, but a big Pearson-Spearman gap is always a warning sign. Next: outliers and anomalies, and what to actually do about them.
